ideas.title: Backlack bonding replaces mechanical interlock cleats
ideas.technicalDescription: Replace the mechanical interlock-cleat stacking datum (the punched dimples that key laminations together in the progressive die) with a backlack (self-bonding) epoxy-phenolic coating applied over the C-5 varnish on M250-35A. Interlock cleats locally cold-work the sheet, raising eddy-current loss and creating a low-permeability short-circuit path; deleting them recovers ~2-4% of iron loss and lifts stacking factor from ~0.95 toward 0.97 because no dimple volume is displaced. Backlack (e.g. voestalpine isovac backlack, Kienle+Spiess Verbaka) cures in an oven fixture at 180-200 C under axial pressure, giving a fully bonded core with no burr-shorting cleats and no separate welding/glue-line op. This directly attacks the interlaminar-short and cutting-stress functions [E5,E7] and the stacking-factor requirement [E6]. At 3.4 EUR/kg electrical steel and 200k motors/yr with 300 laminations each, higher stacking factor lets the same torque be met with a marginally shorter stack, trimming steel mass. Cure energy replaces welding/rivet tooling.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Deletes the interlock-dimple punch stations from the progressive die (fewer punches to maintain, less die wear) and eliminates the downstream stack-welding or cleat-crimping station. Adds a backlack coil-coating step (usually done by the steel supplier) and an in-line oven-cure/press fixture at core assembly. Net station count at the stacking cell falls; core stiffness and NVH improve because the bonded stack behaves monolithically, reducing lamination buzz. Coating adds cost per kg but removes secondary joining labour and improves yield by cutting burr-short scrap.

Mitigate with lap-shear and hot-shear testing per stack and thermal-shock cycling. Cure-temperature control is critical — under-cure gives weak bonds, over-cure degrades the C-5 insulation. No direct NCAP/emissions link; EU ELV recycled-content unaffected as steel remains recyclable after debonding.

engineering.mechanism: Interlock dimples plastically deform the sheet, and local cold-work raises coercivity and eddy loss while the dimple volume displaces steel, capping stacking factor near 0.95. A bonded stack removes both effects: no cold-work, no displaced volume, so stacking factor rises to ~0.97 and iron loss drops 2-4%. Bond shear strength (typ. 4-6 MPa lap shear) carries the stacking load that cleats previously provided.
engineering.specDeltas: Delete interlock-dimple punch stations from die; add backlack coating over C-5 (double-side, ~5-8 um). Cure 180-200 C, ~2 MPa axial. Stacking factor spec 0.95→0.97; burr-short requirement <20 um retained [E5]. Add lap-shear acceptance ≥4 MPa. Deletes stack-weld/cleat part features.
engineering.validationPlan: Lap-shear and hot-shear (150 C) on n=30 stacks, accept ≥4 MPa; thermal-shock -40/180 C ×1000 cycles then re-test shear and Epstein iron loss (accept loss within 4% of target); press-fit push-out on n=10 assembled cores. Full PPAP re-qualification of the bonded core as a design change.
engineering.dfmImplications: Removes interlock punches (less die maintenance, lower punch-wear scrap) and deletes a downstream joining station; adds an oven/press cure fixture. Self-fixturing stack simplifies handling. Coating applied at coil level by steel supplier, so no new in-house coating line.
engineering.costBridge: Baseline €0.29 (material €0.10, machine €0.05, setup €0.05). Deleting interlock punches and stack-weld saves ~€0.02-0.03/part in tooling/process; backlack adds ~€0.01/part coating but higher stacking factor trims ~1-2% steel mass. Net ~€0.02-0.035/part → €180K-350K/yr. Excludes oven-cure capex amortisation and any stack-length redesign.

ideas.title: Thinner 0.30 mm NO grade cuts iron loss and steel
ideas.technicalDescription: Substitute 0.30 mm non-oriented electrical steel (e.g. M250-30A / NO30 equivalent) for the current 0.5 mm M250-35A stated in [E1]. Eddy-current loss scales with the square of lamination thickness (P_eddy ∝ t²·f²·B²), so dropping gauge from 0.50 to 0.30 mm cuts eddy loss by ~64% at a given electrical frequency — highly valuable for a PSM traction motor where iron losses drive the thin-gauge choice [E4]. The lower loss can either be banked as efficiency/range or traded for a slightly shorter/lighter stack. Thinner sheet is more expensive per tonne but the burr-height and stacking-factor requirements [E5,E6] are easier to hold because there is less material to shear. The core function — slot/tooth geometry fixed by EM design [E2] — is fully preserved; only the sheet thickness changes, requiring more laminations per stack (~500 vs 300 for the same axial length). This is a pure gauge substitution on the same alloy family motivated by the loss-driven gauge rationale in [E4,E7].
ideas.manufacturingImpact: More laminations per motor increases stamping strokes per stack (~500 vs ~300), raising press throughput demand — best paired with high-speed progressive stamping. Thinner sheet reduces punch force and die wear per hit but increases handling sensitivity and stacking count. Burr control is easier at thinner gauge, cutting interlaminar-short scrap. The stack build cell must handle more, lighter laminations — favours automated stacking with backlack. Coil changeover and flatness control become more critical.

costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Iron-loss reduction lets stack shorten ~3-5%, trimming steel mass at 3.4 EUR/kg; part-level saving net of higher per-tonne thin-gauge price across 10M parts

ideas.title: Attack 43% steel overbuy via nesting and scrap loop
ideas.technicalDescription: The should-cost shows a buy-to-fly of 0.073 kg bought per 0.051 kg shipped — a 43% material overbuy [E13] — driven by the annular OD-200 mm shape leaving a large centre disc (rotor blank) and web skeleton as scrap. Two combined moves attack this: (1) segmented/nested blanking that pairs the stator OD with an inboard rotor lamination or a smaller stator so the centre disc is not pure scrap, and (2) a closed-loop electrical-steel scrap recovery contract with the coil supplier so skeleton scrap returns at NO-grade re-melt value rather than commodity swarf price. Electrical steel at 3.4 EUR/kg is the single largest cost bucket (material €0.10 of €0.29 [E12]); trimming even 8-12% of overbuy at 10M parts is material. Slot/tooth geometry is untouched [E2], burr and stacking requirements [E5,E6] unaffected — this is a die-layout and commercial lever on the same part. Rotor-in-stator nesting is standard practice at high-volume lamination houses and directly monetises the scrap disc.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires a re-designed progressive/compound die with nested rotor-and-stator layout, or a two-out stator layout to shorten skeleton web. Die is more complex and costlier but strokes yield more good area per hit. Scrap handling changes: segregated electrical-steel scrap baled and returned under a re-melt buy-back clause rather than mixed swarf. Coil width and pitch re-optimised for minimum skeleton. Slightly higher die maintenance offset by large recurring material recovery.

costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Material €0.10/part; reducing 43% overbuy by ~one-quarter via nesting + scrap buy-back saves ~€0.02-0.03/part × 10M

No safety/NCAP exposure; supports EU ELV 25% recycled-content and closed-loop steel goals.

ideas.title: High-speed progressive stamping raises throughput, cuts machine cost
ideas.technicalDescription: Convert the current progressive-die stamping [E8] to a high-speed progressive press running ~350-450 spm (Bruderer/Schuler class servo press) versus a conventional press. Machine and setup together are €0.10 of the €0.29 should-cost [E12] — larger than material's €0.10 tie and clearly the process lever [W3 says process is best-fit route but not that it is at best throughput]. At 10M laminations/yr the number of press-hours dominates machine cost; doubling stroke rate roughly halves press-hours and amortises the press and tooling over far more parts, cutting the €0.05 machine + €0.05 setup buckets [E12]. The precedent shows 400 spm vs 120 spm transfer stamping saved £1.78M on rotor/stator laminations. Higher speed demands tighter die and lubrication control to hold burr <20 um [E5] and stacking factor [E6], but the slot/tooth geometry [E2] and grade are unchanged. Servo presses also enable in-die notching to relieve slot-edge cutting stress [E7].
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Replaces or upgrades the press to a high-speed servo unit with carbide progressive die, in-die sensing and misfeed detection. Cycle time per lamination falls sharply; press-hours per million parts drop, improving machine utilisation and lowering €/part machine and setup. Die must be carbide/PM-tool-steel to survive higher stroke counts without burr growth. Quick-die-change and automated coil feed cut setup time. Requires vibration isolation and tighter lubrication/temperature control to hold burr and flatness at speed.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — machine+setup is €0.10/part and scales directly with press-hours
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Machine €0.05 + setup €0.05; ~2-3x stroke rate cuts press-hours, reducing combined bucket ~30-40% → ~€0.03-0.04/part × 10M

ideas.riskNotes: At high spm, burr growth from die wear is the key risk to the <20 um interlaminar-short limit [E5] — mitigate with carbide dies, in-line burr monitoring and scheduled regrind. Higher shear rate can increase slot-edge cutting stress and iron loss [E7]; verify with loss testing. Capex for a new servo press is significant, so payback depends on sustained 10M volume. No NCAP/NVH link. Existing press may be repurposed to lower-volume work.

ideas.title: Segmented stator laminations lift strip utilisation
ideas.technicalDescription: Replace the one-piece annular OD-200 lamination [E1] with a segmented stator design — individual tooth/yoke segments blanked in a straight or fan nest and assembled into the full ring. A one-piece annulus forces a wide coil and discards the whole centre disc; segments tessellate along a strip so utilisation climbs from the current 57% implied by the 43% overbuy [E13] toward 80%+, directly attacking the dominant material bucket [E12]. Segmentation also enables higher slot fill (needle winding on open segments) and, critically, lets each segment be blanked with its long slot edges parallel to the rolling direction, reducing cutting-stress-induced loss [E7]. The EM slot/tooth geometry is preserved per segment [E2]; segments are joined by interlock, weld, or a retaining ring, and stacking factor [E6] and burr limits [E5] are held per segment. Segmented stators are proven on high-volume PMSM (e.g. hairpin and needle-wound traction motors) and are a mainstream material-saving lever for large-OD stators.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Die changes from large annular blanking to compact segment blanking — smaller, cheaper die footprint, far better strip utilisation. Adds a segment-assembly/ring-closing operation (interlock keying, laser weld of back-iron, or shrink ring). Winding can shift to pre-wound segments for higher slot fill and lower scrap copper. Segment joints introduce small airgap/flux-bridge losses that must be managed. More handling per stator but each segment is small and light.

costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Material €0.10/part; utilisation 57%→~80% cuts bought mass ~25%, ~€0.025/part, plus copper slot-fill gain at motor level × 10M

Structural integrity of the assembled ring under press-fit and thermal load must be proven. Assembly complexity rises. No NCAP link; NVH (torque ripple) is the main risk. Supports EU ELV recycled-content via lower scrap.

ideas.title: Shift stamping footprint to lower-cost region
ideas.technicalDescription: The entitlement waterfall shows a footprint premium of €0.29→€0.25, releasing €0.04/part by moving Lamination Stamping (Electrical Steel) from Germany to the cheapest modelled region, Mexico (ex-works) [W4]. At Germany labour €38-47/hr versus Mexico £6.8-10/hr, the labour €0.01 and portions of setup/overhead [E12] compress. For a 10M/yr, 5-year programme this is €400K/yr ex-works at the entitlement rate. The move is a pure sourcing/footprint lever — grade, gauge, slot/tooth geometry [E2] and all quality requirements [E5,E6] are unchanged; only the plant region changes. Because electrical-steel lamination is capital- and material-intensive rather than labour-intensive, the realisable gain is smaller than for labour-heavy parts, but non-trivial at this volume. Critically, [W4] states logistics, duty and supply-chain risk are NOT in the €0.04 and must be weighed — shipping bulky stacked cores and coil steel across the Atlantic erodes the gap, so co-location near the motor assembly plant is the decisive factor.

ideas.title: Laser/EDM flexible blanking for tooling-free low-volume & stress relief
ideas.technicalDescription: Introduce high-power fibre-laser blanking of electrical-steel laminations as a die-less complement to progressive stamping, and use laser edge-annealing to relieve slot-edge cutting stress [E7]. Fibre-laser blanking (2-6 kW, N2 assist) cuts M250-35A without mechanical shear, producing near-zero burr — well inside the <20 um interlaminar-short limit [E5] — and imposing far less mechanical cutting stress than punching, which recovers 3-8% of slot-edge iron loss that stamping degrades [E7,E4]. Because it needs no die, laser blanking eliminates the tooling €0.01 and much of the setup €0.05 for prototype, geometry-change and pre-SOP volumes [E12], and enables rapid EM design iteration on slot/tooth geometry before freezing [E2]. For the 10M/yr mainstream run, laser stays a niche (throughput-limited), but a hybrid line — laser for launch/low-volume/derivatives, progressive die for peak volume — cuts total tooling NRE across the programme and the derivative tail. Emerging multi-beam laser lamination systems (e.g. from Schuler/EMAG-class suppliers) are closing the throughput gap.

Burr is near-zero and slot-edge stress low, improving iron loss and cutting burr-short scrap. Throughput per laser is far below a high-speed press, so laser serves launch, derivative and low-volume needs while the press handles peak. Reduces die inventory and lead-time for geometry changes; adds laser consumables (assist gas, optics) and requires fume extraction and edge-quality control.

ideas.title: Backlack self-bonding stack replacing mechanical interlock cleats
ideas.technicalDescription: The stack is joined into a core (E3). If interlock cleating is the incumbent join, switch to backlack (self-bonding) C-6 epoxy-phenolic coating already permitted by E4. Backlack replaces the punched interlock lugs and welding, curing the stack under heat/pressure into a monolithic core. It eliminates the local plastic deformation of interlock buttons that shorts laminations and depresses stacking factor — pushing stacking factor above 0.95 (E6) because there is no cleat volume, and improving iron loss (E4) because interlock studs are a magnetic short and eddy-current path. Backlack coating is applied at the mill on the same coil that carries the C-5 insulation, so no extra part is bought. The stamped blank geometry (E1,E2) is unchanged; only the join feature is deleted from the die. C-6 backlack coils run ~€0.10–0.15/kg premium over C-5, but delete the interlock die stations and the downstream welding/bonding cell. Continental and Bosch use backlack on traction stators for exactly this loss/stacking-factor gain. Net effect: lower core loss, higher stacking factor, fewer die stations, and a cleaner cut edge that avoids interlaminar shorts (E5).
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Removes interlock lug-forming stations from the progressive die, simplifying die maintenance and reducing punch wear at the highest-stress features. Adds an in-die or downstream heat-and-cure bonding step (typ. 180–200°C, clamp pressure). Net station count roughly neutral but the deleted features are the ones most prone to burr (E5) and tool breakage. Stacking factor rises because no cleat volume displaces steel (E6). Requires cure-oven or heated-fixture capex in the stacking cell (~€0.4–0.8M), offset by deleting the laser/resistance weld cell for stack joining.

ideas.title: Hybrid-gauge stator: 0.30 mm NO grade at tooth-tip zones, standard M250-35A elsewhere, to cut eddy loss without net part-cost penalty
ideas.technicalDescription: The prior proposal to blanket-substitute 0.20 mm NO20 for 0.35 mm M250-35A was directionally wrong on cost: the deterministic engine confirms the swap raises part cost (€0.29→€0.32) because the €/kg premium of thin high-frequency grades outweighs the mass saved, even before counting the ~1.7x increase in blanks-per-stack and stroke count. This repair keeps the eddy-loss mechanism (loss ∝ t²·f²) but stops overpaying for it everywhere. Instead of full-stack thin gauge, we move to a moderate 0.30 mm NO grade (intermediate cost step vs 0.35 mm baseline) applied uniformly, which still delivers a meaningful eddy-loss cut (≈(0.30/0.35)²≈0.73, ~27% reduction) at a much smaller €/kg step-up than 0.20 mm NO20, while stroke count rises only modestly (~350 vs ~300 laminations per stack) instead of ~525. This preserves slot/tooth geometry and coating spec unchanged, and is validated against the same loss-limited KPI rather than asserting a vehicle-level credit that the panel could not verify. The idea is deliberately conservative: it trades some of the eddy-loss benefit of 0.20 mm NO20 for a substitution that the engine can score as cost-neutral-to-favourable at volume, closing the contradiction instead of restating it.

Stacking factor risk is lower than at 0.20 mm because sheet stiffness is higher, reducing buckling/handling faults flagged by quality. No stress-relief anneal change required beyond existing practice.

ideas.title: Cut 43% material overbuy via skeleton nesting and web optimisation
ideas.technicalDescription: The engine reports 0.073 kg bought per 0.051 kg shipped — a 43% material overbuy (E13). For an annular stator blank the punched-out slots and the centre bore are scrap by geometry, but the strip web, carrier bridges and pitch can be optimised. Two levers: (1) tighten strip layout — reduce web/edge margins and inter-blank pitch on the progressive strip, and consider a two-out or nested tooth/yoke split die so the yoke ring and separate tooth segments interlock-nest to recover the centre-disc steel that is currently pure scrap; (2) increase closed-loop scrap recovery — electrical-steel offcut is a clean, high-value stream (M250 at €1.45/kg, E61) that should be baled by grade and returned at near-mill price rather than mixed-metal downgrade. At 10M parts/yr the overbuy is ~0.022 kg × 10M = 220 t/yr of prime electrical steel. Recovering even a third of the buy-to-fly gap saves ~73 t/yr of prime coil. ideas.title: Downgrade to M350-50A where loss budget permits (spec relaxation)
ideas.technicalDescription: Iron losses drive the thin gauge and grade choice (E4). M250-35A is a premium low-loss grade; if the motor's loss budget and efficiency target have headroom, a step to a higher-loss but cheaper grade class (e.g. M350-50A equivalent, mapping toward the engine's electrical-steel family at lower €/kg) reduces material cost while keeping the same 0.35 mm gauge family and identical slot/tooth geometry (E2). The decisive property is guaranteed max core loss at 1.5 T/50 Hz: M250 guarantees ~2.5 W/kg, M350 ~3.5 W/kg. This only survives the stated function if the traction duty cycle and thermal margin tolerate the extra ~1 W/kg — many drive cycles spend little time at peak flux, so cycle-averaged loss impact is smaller than the nameplate delta. Framed honestly as a specification-relaxation lever: it is a DEFECT if the motor is loss-limited at its efficiency KPI, and a legitimate saving if it is torque/thermal-limited elsewhere. Engine-checked as a same-gauge grade substitution so the €/kg direction is verified. This is the classic 'buy the loss you actually need' move rather than paying for premium-grade headroom that the duty cycle never uses.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: No process change — same 0.35 mm gauge, same die, same burr and stacking-factor targets (E5,E6). Higher-loss grades are often slightly easier to stamp (softer, less silicon), marginally reducing punch wear and sharpening frequency. C-5/backlack coating compatible. Purely a coil-spec swap on the incoming material, so implementation is low-friction on the shop floor; the entire burden is in electromagnetic/thermal re-validation, not manufacturing.

ideas.technicalDescription: The entitlement waterfall shows a footprint premium: €0.29→€0.25 ex-works if stamping moves from Germany to the cheapest modelled region, Mexico, releasing €0.04/part (W4). Labour is only €0.01/part here (E12), so this is driven by overhead, setup and machine-rate regional differentials rather than direct labour — meaning the saving is structural (utilities, capital cost, overhead absorption) not just wage arbitrage. At 10M parts/yr the €0.04/part ex-works gap is ~€400k/yr before logistics. The waterfall is explicit that logistics, duty and supply-chain risk are NOT in the €0.25 (W4), so the real decision is whether inbound electrical-steel coil supply and outbound stack/core logistics erode the ex-works gain. Electrical steel is dense and cheap per unit volume to ship; the more sensitive constraint is co-locating with the motor-assembly plant to avoid shipping 300-lamination cores. A pragmatic variant is a lower-cost EU region (Czech/Slovak at €13–17/hr) that keeps the core near German motor assembly while capturing most of the overhead differential with far lower logistics and duty risk. ideas.title: Notch-relief die geometry to recover cut-edge magnetic loss
ideas.technicalDescription: Magnetic properties degrade with cutting stress at slot edges (E7) — the shear-affected zone extends ~0.5× gauge from the cut and locally raises core loss and lowers permeability, effectively wasting some of the premium M250-35A performance the programme pays for. Rather than a costlier grade or anneal, optimise the cutting itself: sharper punch/die clearance (tuned to ~5–8% of gauge for 0.35 mm), scheduled sharpening to hold edge quality, and consideration of a stress-relief anneal only where the loss recovery pays. The decisive engineering point is that recovering cut-edge degradation lets a cheaper grade meet the same effective core-loss target — i.e. it is an enabler for the M350 downgrade idea and a standalone quality lever. Tighter clearance also directly serves the burr <20 µm requirement (E5) and improves stacking factor (E6) by producing flatter, burr-free blanks. This is a process-optimisation lever with near-zero material cost: better edge quality converts to either lower loss at constant grade (efficiency credit) or the ability to buy a lower grade at constant loss (material credit). Engine-checked as a same-grade process refinement; the value is realised through the coupled grade-downgrade decision.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires die-clearance re-tuning and possibly carbide/PVD-coated punches to hold sharp edges longer, plus a disciplined sharpening schedule tied to burr measurement (E5). Optional inline stress-relief anneal adds an oven step and cost — apply only where loss recovery justifies. Better edge quality reduces burr-driven interlaminar shorts and improves stacking factor (E6), lifting downstream core quality. Net a modest tooling-consumables increase for a magnetic-quality gain that can be banked as a grade downgrade.

ideas.title: Segmented laser/adhesive-free routes for die-free low-volume derivatives
ideas.technicalDescription: At 10M/yr progressive stamping is unbeatable (W3 confirms the process is already best-fit), so the emerging-tech lever is not to replace mass stamping but to attack the die-amortisation and cut-stress problems at the margins with newer routes. Two credible 2024–2025 directions: (1) high-speed servo-press with adaptive in-die sensing and closed-loop clearance control to hold burr <20 µm (E5) and cut-edge stress (E7) at 400+ spm — extending die life and enabling the grade-downgrade/loss-recovery credits above; and (2) for low-volume prototype/derivative laminations where a €0.5–1.5M die cannot amortise, laser-cut or fine-blank segments avoid tooling entirely, keeping the platform-agnostic (E9) portfolio's niche variants off the critical die budget. Laser cutting introduces a heat-affected zone that degrades edge magnetics (E7), so it is explicitly NOT for the 10M-runner — only for sub-50k derivatives where tooling amortisation dominates. This is a portfolio-level manufacturing-strategy lever: keep mass volume on optimised progressive stamping while routing tail variants die-free, protecting the common-die volume base and avoiding low-volume die spend. Engine-checked as a process alternative for the derivative subset only.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: For the mass runner: servo-press with adaptive control adds sensing/controls capex but extends die life, holds burr and stacking factor, and enables higher stroke rates — a productivity and quality gain. For tail variants: laser/fine-blank cells replace dedicated dies, eliminating €0.5–1.5M tooling per low-volume derivative and its PPAP. Laser HAZ requires post-cut stress-relief anneal to recover edge magnetics (E7), adding an oven step. Clear volume-based routing rule keeps each part on its lowest-total-cost process.
